Thirty thousand years ago,
people in Ice Age
Europe pressed their hands
against cave walls and
blew pigment around them.
Researchers studied more
than five hundred of
these stencils from
twenty-six caves in France
and Spain.
About three quarters were
left hands.
What does that tell
us about the artists?
It fits a simple picture.
Most artists held the
pigment in their right
hand and pressed the
free left hand against
the rock.
Even in the Ice
Age, the right hand
was usually the busy one.
And the evidence goes
back much further than art.
In a cave pit
in northern Spain called
the Sima de los
Huesos, researchers studied
the front teeth of
early relatives of the
Neanderthals, who lived
more than four hundred
thousand years ago.
These people seem to
have gripped meat between
their teeth and sliced
it with a stone tool.
The angle of the
tiny scratches shows which
hand held the tool.
In all fifteen individuals
they studied, it was
the right.
Neanderthal teeth tell
the same story,
and so do their
arm bones, which grew
thicker on the side
that worked harder.
Together, these clues
suggest that roughly nine
out of ten Neanderthals
were right-handed, about
the same share as
people today.
The ratio seems to
be older than our own species.
Language kept a record
of how people felt
about the two hands.
In Latin, the word
for left was sinister,
and in English it
came to mean threatening
or evil.
The Latin word for
right, dexter, gave us
dexterity, meaning skill.
In French, gauche means
left, and it also
means clumsy.
For a long time,
that preference was enforced.
Well into the twentieth
century, many schools in
Europe, North America and
East Asia made left-handed
children write with their
right hand.
Some teachers tied a
child's left hand behind
the chair, or rapped
their knuckles with a ruler.
Many grew up as
switched right-handers.
Then, as the pressure
eased, the numbers changed.
Surveys of Americans born
around 1900 found only
about three percent who
called themselves left-handed.
Among people born in
the second half of
the century, the share
climbed to roughly eleven
or twelve percent.
It wasn't a fashion spreading.
Children were simply no
longer being forced to
hide it.
So the next time
you see someone writing
with their left hand,
think of the long
story behind it,
from Ice Age cave
walls to tied-down classroom
chairs.
The full story,
and why the share
stays near ten percent,
is on Miya's Lab.
